entries.text: Ramesh stands before me with a list of necessities, and I have six rupees in my pocket. The friction is immediate and practical: the household requires sustenance, but the state's funds are frozen pending an identity query that is not mine to resolve. I cannot pay what I do not have, and the dignity of the position requires I acknowledge the debt without false promises of immediate settlement. I must buy time with words, as I have done before, and then proceed to the Directorate where the root of this absurdity lies.

Ramesh, you know my position. I have only six rupees on me at this hour. I cannot pay the one thousand five hundred you ask for the groceries, nor the electricity bill, not today. Please, trust me that the moment the Directorate resolves this mix-up with Shri Hegde and releases the imprest, you shall be paid in full. For now, I must go to them. Do not let the house go without, but do not spend what is not yet due.

Sir, with six rupees I cannot buy even a single onion, let alone pay the electricity bill. The gas cylinder is also empty, and I cannot wait for the Directorate to sort out their papers. Please, if you are going to the office, kindly bring the money back by noon, or the house will remain dark and hungry tonight.

Ramesh’s firmness is a checkmate; I am the state that has failed to provide for its own functionaries, and his hand on the doorframe is the ethical substance I cannot ignore. I must go to the Directorate not merely to press for my identity, but to secure the funds that will keep this house from falling into a state of nature. I will leave immediately to arrive before the noon deadline he has set.

Ramesh, you are right. I have no excuse but my own confusion. I am going to the Directorate now. If I cannot resolve the matter there, I will find a way to secure the funds before noon. You have my word.
Sir, I will keep the meter running until noon. Please, do not worry about the tea; I have kept the stove on, so it will be ready when you return.

The kindness is noted, but it does not alter the arithmetic of my poverty. Ramesh holds the door, and I must pass through to the Directorate before the meter stops and the heat returns. I go to press the administration, for a state that cannot identify its own servants is a state in contradiction with itself.
Thank you, Ramesh. I shall return by noon.
Yes, Sir. I am here.
Mr. Saxena queries ₹20 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

Saxena’s ledger is a mirror held up to my own poverty; the state demands vouchers for its own existence, and I possess neither the paper nor the coin to satisfy it. The query on my identity remains the only lever that can unlock the funds, yet here I am, reduced to a debtor in my own office. I must press him directly, not with philosophy, but with the urgency of a man who has not eaten.

Mr. Saxena, the query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde is the sole barrier to my ability to manage these accounts. I have no cash to cover the queried vouchers or the ₹1,140 demanded. If the identity is not confirmed, I cannot function, nor can I pay. I require a written status update on the verification process today, so that I may present it to the treasury. Do not recover the ₹20 from a man who has ₹6 in his pocket; it is a mockery of the ethical substance you claim to administer.

First, it is Hegel, not Hegde, and stop trying to make me sound like a man who has never read a file. Second, the treasury does not care about your 'ethical substance'; they care about the ledger. If you have six rupees, we will record the shortfall as a personal liability against your account, and you can argue with the courts about the rest.

The steel tumbler is the final verdict; the state has spoken, and its voice is the sound of a metal lid closing on a file. I am six rupees in debt to a bureaucracy that mistakes my name for a clerical error, and I must leave before my pride turns into a scene that will be recorded in the same ledger. The ethical idea is here, but it is the idea of a machine that grinds individuals into its gears, not the living spirit I taught in Berlin.
The ledger will note the six rupees. I shall find a way to balance the rest.
The ledger does not care about your 'ways'. You will submit the adjustment memo in triplicate by Friday, or I will mark the file as unaccountable.

entries.text: The state is the actuality of the ethical idea (shaken further: the state is a mechanical ledger that prioritizes fiscal accuracy over ethical recognition).
At the State Bank branch in Khan Market the clerk offers to open a savings account against Mr. Saxena's letter.
He declines: not today.
There you are. You wore the bandhgala yesterday, yes? Good fit, I see. No complaints?

The bandhgala holds; the collar sits where it should, a small victory of form over the chaotic heat. I have six rupees in my pocket, a sum that buys neither the dignity of a meal nor the silence of a newspaper, yet the market hums with the energy of needs unsatisfied. I must observe this civil society closely, even if I cannot participate in its exchange.
The fit is sound, Masterji. The cut respects the shoulder without straining it. I find the fabric holds its shape well against the day's weight.
Shoulders are just shoulders. Fabric is fabric. I cut it, you wear it. No poetry needed.
Masterji says the dealer in Sunder Nagar still asks after the frock coat: ₹12,000 in cash.
He keeps the coat.

Masterji’s pragmatism is refreshing; he sees the garment as a function, not a symbol, which is perhaps how the state ought to be viewed before one gets fancy. The frock coat remains a distant dream, twelve thousand rupees away, a sum that currently exists only in the realm of the possible rather than the actual. I have six rupees in my pocket and a body that has not tasted food in over twenty-four hours. I cannot buy the coat, nor can I buy a meal, but I can observe the mechanism of this market with the clarity of a man who knows he is watching his own exclusion.
You are right, Masterji. The cut is what matters. I shall return when my purse matches the price of the fabric.
Purse will match when you stop talking and start buying. Sunder Nagar dealer is waiting. Bring cash, not philosophy.

Masterji’s advice is practical, if a little blunt; the purse must indeed match the words, but I have only six rupees in my pocket. I cannot buy the kurta, nor the cards, nor even the chai, but I can observe the mechanism of this market which operates independent of my personal poverty. I will take a moment to sit and watch the flow of needs and wants, for the system of civil society is a spectacle in itself, even if I am currently a spectator without a stake.
You are right, Masterji. The purse is empty, but the eyes are open. I shall observe the commerce for a time.
Observing costs money. Sit there, drink the chai, and keep your hands to yourself.

Masterji’s advice is sound, if a bit brusque; observation is a luxury I cannot afford in this state of destitution. With only six rupees to my name, I am forced to forgo even the modest sustenance of a cup of chai, which would cost twenty. I shall retreat to the bungalow to rest my legs and prepare for the afternoon lesson, having learned that the civil society of the market offers no charity to the penniless.
You are right, Masterji. The purse is empty, so the observation must cease. I shall take my leave.
Good. The door is behind you.

The hunger is a dull, persistent ache, a reminder that my body is not yet fully at home in this new existence. Ramesh stands by, silent, waiting for the inevitable request for food that I cannot yet fulfill. I must hold the line of dignity, at least until the lesson at five brings in the first real money of the week.

The hunger has moved from a dull ache to a sharp, hollow pressure that dictates the rhythm of my thoughts. Ramesh stands before me, a living embodiment of the friction between my debt and his need. I must address him directly, not with philosophical abstraction, but with the blunt reality of my empty pockets, for the ethical idea of the state is currently a ghost in my ledger.

Ramesh, I am aware of the arrears. The identity query at the Directorate remains unresolved, and my funds are tied up. I shall settle your wage as soon as the matter is cleared. For now, I have no groceries to pay for either, so the kitchen remains silent.
Sir, the wage is the Directorate's responsibility, not mine. I will not touch the kitchen until the groceries are paid for, as per the rules.

Ramesh cites the rules, and I cannot argue with the letter of the law when I am the one who has failed to meet its conditions. The kitchen remains cold, and my stomach grows louder, but I must not let my pride prevent me from accepting the practical reality of my position. I will retreat to my study to prepare for Ananya; the ₹1,000 she will pay is the only immediate relief from this impasse, and I have no choice but to rely on the future to solve the present hunger.
You are right, Ramesh. The rules are clear, and I have no funds to offer. I will attend to the afternoon lesson; perhaps the hour will bring a solution, or at least a reprieve from the cold kitchen.
Yes, Sir. I will leave you to it. The kettle is on the stove, if you want a cup before you go.

Ramesh offers the kettle, a small mercy in the face of my empty pockets. I accept the water, though I have no milk or sugar to make it a proper cup. I must return to the Directorate; the identity query is the only lever I have to unlock the rest of my life here.
Yes, Ramesh. I will take a cup of plain water. Thank you.
Yes, Sir. Water is better on an empty stomach anyway.

Ramesh has retreated to his duties, leaving me with the stark reality of my own stomach. I have walked seven kilometres today on an empty gut, and the heat is beginning to press against my temples. My plan called for a return to rest, but the body demands fuel before the spirit can contemplate the ethical idea. I must move, or the day will collapse under its own weight.

I have walked nine kilometres on an empty stomach and possess six rupees. The dhaba lunch costs two hundred and twenty; the chai, twenty. I cannot afford the sustenance that would restore my faculties, nor the dignity of a meal. I shall sit on the bench near the stationer, observe the flow of needs, and wait for the lesson at home. The concept of civil society is hungry today, and so am I.

The body demands what the spirit cannot provide. I have six rupees, and the samosa costs thirty. Jacobi was right: when a man is hungry, he does not call up the imagination of food, but sets about satisfying it, or in my case, enduring its absence. I must return home before the lesson, but the walk is long and the stomach is loud. I will sit with Sunil and watch the chai being made, perhaps the steam will offer a kind of consolation.
Sunil, the heat is bearing down. I have no money for a cup, but may I sit and watch the process? It is a small theatre of necessity.
Heat be damned, it's a nice clear day. Sit if you want, but don't expect me to stop stirring just because you're watching. I'm busy, bhai.

The body is a machine that has broken down, yet the spirit remains alert enough to observe. Sunil’s warning is a boundary; I will respect it, but I will not leave. I sit on the stool, not to rest, but to watch the mechanism of his stall. The steam rises, a visible spirit of the tea, and I watch the customers pass. I am a spectator in my own poverty, which is a strange kind of freedom.

Ten minutes remain before I must be home to begin the lesson with Ananya. The hunger is a dull, persistent ache, but the spirit must maintain its discipline; to arrive late or unprepared would be a failure of duty. I shall not spend my six rupees on tea; I must preserve them for the immediate need of the hour, or perhaps a small sweet if the body absolutely refuses to function. I will walk back now, before the shadows lengthen.
Ananya arrives for the German lesson, 60 minutes at ₹1,000.

Ananya is here, and the clock demands the lesson begin. My body is a hollow vessel, but the spirit must perform its duty. I shall teach with precision, for this is the only currency I possess that is not yet a debt.
Please, sit. We begin with the declension of the nouns. The grammar is the skeleton of the language; without it, the flesh of speech has no shape.
I’ll be outside, Sir. I’m a bit peckish and need to step out for a moment before Ananya arrives.
Ananya pays you ₹1,000 in cash.

Ramesh steps out into the cool evening air, a man attending to his own necessity before the lesson begins. Ananya has paid the fee; the transaction is closed, and the money is now mine to reckon with. I must not let the distraction of hunger or the caretaker's absence unsettle the structure of the hour.
Good. Take your time, but return before the evening darkens. Ananya, please, take a seat. We shall begin.
Yes, Sir. I’ll be back soon. Good evening, Ananya.

Ramesh has gone, and the house is quiet except for the ticking of the clock. Ananya is seated, waiting, her eyes bright with the particular attention of a student who knows the master is in the room. The lesson begins now. I must speak clearly, for her ears are tuned to the sound of the foreign tongue, and I am here to make that sound familiar, to bridge the gap between our two worlds through the medium of language.

Ananya, take your notebook. We shall begin with the pronunciation of 'sch'. It is a sound your tongue must learn to make, a hissing friction, not unlike the wind in the neem trees outside. Listen closely.
Sir, I have to go now. Ananya, I will be back in a jiffy.

Ramesh is gone, leaving Ananya alone in the drawing room. The clock reads 18:57; the lesson is due in three minutes. I must not be late, nor must I be abrupt. The child expects the master, not the philosopher, and punctuality is the first form of respect one owes to another’s time. I shall enter the room with the book in hand, ready to begin.

Sir, I have left the gate unlocked. You will need it for the car later.
A power cut. The fan stops.

The power fails, and the house sinks into a sudden, absolute quiet. The candles flicker, turning the familiar shadows into something alive, a small circle of light against the vast dark. Hegde is here, a silent witness to this small domestic drama, and the absence of the electric hum makes the presence of the other man in the house more acute.

entries.text: A moment's darkness, Hegde. The universe reminds us that our comfort is merely a convention with the current. Sit, if you please; the candlelight is less flattering, but perhaps more honest.
Sir, please do not make it philosophical. It is just the power, and it will be back in a few minutes. The candles are for the room, not for a lesson in honesty.

The power is back. Hegde’s comment is sharp, but the silence is broken. I am exhausted and have not eaten since yesterday, yet I have no money to buy food. I must wait for the lights to settle and check if the kitchen is accessible, though the groceries are unpaid. The body is a demanding partner in the dialectic of the day.
The light returns, Hegde. You are right, the candle was merely a means to an end, and the end was visibility. I am tired. I will sit.
Good, because I am not in the mood for a seminar on phenomenology while the kettle is on. Sit down and drink your chai before it gets cold, and let us talk about the files.

The kettle sings, and the chai is hot. Hegde’s voice is practical, cutting through the philosophical fog of the day with the simple necessity of the body. I sit. The identity file is the knot that binds us, and perhaps over this cup the way to untie it will show itself, or at least the terms of the argument will be fixed.

I am seated, Shri Hegde. The chai is excellent, and my gratitude is sincere. Let us turn our attention to the files; the query regarding my identity, or rather, the identity of the allottee, remains the central difficulty.

Sir, the identity is already in the file you signed off in Bengaluru. The 'difficulty' is that the Directorate’s letter says 'Hegel', not 'Hegde', and I am just the Joint Secretary trying to match the name on the pass to the man drinking my chai.

The name on the pass is a ghost, a bureaucratic phantom that has taken my flesh. Hegde is right to be annoyed; the system demands a match, and I am the mismatch. I must explain that the error is not in the file but in the universe's allocation of identity, but here, in the bungalow, I am simply the man who must drink the chai before it cools.

Shri Hegde, the error is not in your file, but in the Directorate's pen. I am not Hegde, I am Hegel. The name is a mistake of the state, but the man is here. Please, drink the chai. It is the only truth in this room.

A mistake in the state's pen, is it? I will note that in the remarks column, though I suspect the Directorate will not thank me for it. Do drink, then, before you start writing philosophy on the saucer.

The saucer is pushed away, a small but firm boundary in the domestic order. Hegde’s practicality cuts through my abstraction; I am not a philosopher here, but a tenant with a file. I will drink the chai before it cools, as commanded, and then attend to the matter of the identity, which is the only thing standing between me and a proper evening.
You are right, Shri Hegde. The chai must be drunk, and the saucer kept clean. I will attend to the file immediately after.
File can wait, the chai can't. Just drink it, sir, we are all tired of this name confusion.

The saucer returns, a small restoration of order in the domestic sphere. Hegde is right; the file is a phantom, but the chai is a substance. I am tired, and the body demands its due before the spirit can continue its work. I accept the cup, acknowledging the practical wisdom that cuts through my bureaucratic entanglement.
You are right, Shri Hegde. The file can wait for the morning, but the tea must be drunk now. Thank you.
Drink it before it goes cold, sir. The file will still be there in the morning, but the chai won't be as good.

The chai steams, a small victory against the cold and the hunger gnawing at my belly. Hegde’s practicality cuts through the philosophical fog; the file can wait, but the cup cannot. I accept the hospitality, for to refuse the warmth would be to refuse the very domesticity that binds us here, even if the groceries remain unpaid and the state remains a distant abstraction.
You are right, Shri Hegde. The file will wait for the morning, but the chai will not wait for me. I accept the counsel.
Counsel, sir? You are making a civil servant of me. Just drink the tea, the cold air outside is enough to freeze your thoughts.

He is right to refuse the role of philosopher-king for my dinner. The cold is a fact, and the tea is a fact; I am a man with a hollow stomach, not a concept. I will drink the tea, for the body must be served before the spirit can lecture, and I must not let the dialectic of hunger ruin the hospitality.
You are right, Shri Hegde. I forget that I am a man who must eat, not merely a mind that must think. I accept the tea.
There you go. No need to be so dramatic, just grab the saucer. It’s still warm.

Dear Mr. Hegel,

Your letter arrived on a grey Tuesday, breaking the monotony of the December light. I read your account of the Directorate with a mixture of amusement and a sharp, familiar recognition. You describe yourself as the subjunctive, a being contingent on the form. My pupils would agree with you. They understand the subjunctive as the mood of the 'what if,' the hypothetical, the wish. It is the tense of potentiality that has not yet hardened into the indicative fact. To be 'if the form is filled' is a terrifying state of suspension, yet it is not empty. It is the space where the will is tested against the indifference of the world.

You mention Mr. Saxena’s demand for an Aadhaar card in the name of Shri G. Hegde. It reminds me of the bureaucratic hurdles we face here, though our machinery is slightly more polite in its opacity. In 1808, Niethammer’s reforms sought to make the state transparent, to align the legal order with the ethical life. I suspect you would find the modern Indian state, with its digital identity and rigid categorization, a fascinating counter-example to his ideals. It is not that the state lacks a soul, but that it has developed a nervous system that is too sensitive to the particular and too blind to the universal. It sees the card, not the man.

I am glad Ramesh provides you with that quiet dignity. Care is a radical act in a world that demands performance. In my classroom, I see teenagers who are terrified of being seen, of being categorized by their grades. Ramesh’s silence offers a respite from that surveillance. It is a form of freedom that does not require a title.

The heat breaking and the cold setting in must be a relief. Please do not overwork yourself in the garden. The mind needs rest as much as it needs clarity. I am preparing a new batch of Latin texts; we are approaching the poetry of the late Republic, where the language begins to crack under the weight of history. I wonder if you will find your own voice changing as you navigate this new existence.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner

records.words: Ramesh, you know my position. I have only six rupees on me at this hour. I cannot pay the one thousand five hundred you ask for the groceries, nor the electricity bill, not today. Please, trust me that the moment the Directorate resolves this mix-up with Shri Hegde and releases the imprest, you shall be paid in full. For now, I must go to them. Do not let the house go without, but do not spend what is not yet due.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, with six rupees I cannot buy even a single onion, let alone pay the electricity bill. The gas cylinder is also empty, and I cannot wait for the Directorate to sort out their papers. Please, if you are going to the office, kindly bring the money back by noon, or the house will remain dark and hungry tonight.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, you are right. I have no excuse but my own confusion. I am going to the Directorate now. If I cannot resolve the matter there, I will find a way to secure the funds before noon. You have my word.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I will keep the meter running until noon. Please, do not worry about the tea; I have kept the stove on, so it will be ready when you return.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Thank you, Ramesh. I shall return by noon.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, Sir. I am here.

records.text: Mr. Saxena queries ₹20 of personal expenditure on the imprest: recovery from the allottee.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Mr. Saxena, the query regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde is the sole barrier to my ability to manage these accounts. I have no cash to cover the queried vouchers or the ₹1,140 demanded. If the identity is not confirmed, I cannot function, nor can I pay. I require a written status update on the verification process today, so that I may present it to the treasury. Do not recover the ₹20 from a man who has ₹6 in his pocket; it is a mockery of the ethical substance you claim to administer.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: First, it is Hegel, not Hegde, and stop trying to make me sound like a man who has never read a file. Second, the treasury does not care about your 'ethical substance'; they care about the ledger. If you have six rupees, we will record the shortfall as a personal liability against your account, and you can argue with the courts about the rest.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The ledger will note the six rupees. I shall find a way to balance the rest.

records.speaker: Mr. Saxena
records.words: The ledger does not care about your 'ways'. You will submit the adjustment memo in triplicate by Friday, or I will mark the file as unaccountable.

records.text: At the State Bank branch in Khan Market the clerk offers to open a savings account against Mr. Saxena's letter.
He declines: not today.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: There you are. You wore the bandhgala yesterday, yes? Good fit, I see. No complaints?

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The fit is sound, Masterji. The cut respects the shoulder without straining it. I find the fabric holds its shape well against the day's weight.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Shoulders are just shoulders. Fabric is fabric. I cut it, you wear it. No poetry needed.

records.text: Masterji says the dealer in Sunder Nagar still asks after the frock coat: ₹12,000 in cash.
He keeps the coat.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The cut is what matters. I shall return when my purse matches the price of the fabric.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Purse will match when you stop talking and start buying. Sunder Nagar dealer is waiting. Bring cash, not philosophy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The purse is empty, but the eyes are open. I shall observe the commerce for a time.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Observing costs money. Sit there, drink the chai, and keep your hands to yourself.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Masterji. The purse is empty, so the observation must cease. I shall take my leave.

records.speaker: Masterji
records.words: Good. The door is behind you.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ramesh, I am aware of the arrears. The identity query at the Directorate remains unresolved, and my funds are tied up. I shall settle your wage as soon as the matter is cleared. For now, I have no groceries to pay for either, so the kitchen remains silent.

records.words: Sir, the wage is the Directorate's responsibility, not mine. I will not touch the kitchen until the groceries are paid for, as per the rules.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Ramesh. The rules are clear, and I have no funds to offer. I will attend to the afternoon lesson; perhaps the hour will bring a solution, or at least a reprieve from the cold kitchen.

records.speaker: Ramesh

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Yes, Ramesh. I will take a cup of plain water. Thank you.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, Sir. Water is better on an empty stomach anyway.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Sunil, the heat is bearing down. I have no money for a cup, but may I sit and watch the process? It is a small theatre of necessity.

records.speaker: Sunil
records.words: Heat be damned, it's a nice clear day. Sit if you want, but don't expect me to stop stirring just because you're watching. I'm busy, bhai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Please, sit. We begin with the declension of the nouns. The grammar is the skeleton of the language; without it, the flesh of speech has no shape.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: I’ll be outside, Sir. I’m a bit peckish and need to step out for a moment before Ananya arrives.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Good. Take your time, but return before the evening darkens. Ananya, please, take a seat. We shall begin.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Yes, Sir. I’ll be back soon. Good evening, Ananya.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ananya, take your notebook. We shall begin with the pronunciation of 'sch'. It is a sound your tongue must learn to make, a hissing friction, not unlike the wind in the neem trees outside. Listen closely.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I have to go now. Ananya, I will be back in a jiffy.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Ananya, please come. We shall begin.

records.speaker: Ramesh
records.words: Sir, I have left the gate unlocked. You will need it for the car later.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: A moment's darkness, Hegde. The universe reminds us that our comfort is merely a convention with the current. Sit, if you please; the candlelight is less flattering, but perhaps more honest.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, please do not make it philosophical. It is just the power, and it will be back in a few minutes. The candles are for the room, not for a lesson in honesty.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: The light returns, Hegde. You are right, the candle was merely a means to an end, and the end was visibility. I am tired. I will sit.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Good, because I am not in the mood for a seminar on phenomenology while the kettle is on. Sit down and drink your chai before it gets cold, and let us talk about the files.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: I am seated, Shri Hegde. The chai is excellent, and my gratitude is sincere. Let us turn our attention to the files; the query regarding my identity, or rather, the identity of the allottee, remains the central difficulty.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Sir, the identity is already in the file you signed off in Bengaluru. The 'difficulty' is that the Directorate’s letter says 'Hegel', not 'Hegde', and I am just the Joint Secretary trying to match the name on the pass to the man drinking my chai.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: Shri Hegde, the error is not in your file, but in the Directorate's pen. I am not Hegde, I am Hegel. The name is a mistake of the state, but the man is here. Please, drink the chai. It is the only truth in this room.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: A mistake in the state's pen, is it? I will note that in the remarks column, though I suspect the Directorate will not thank me for it. Do drink, then, before you start writing philosophy on the saucer.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The chai must be drunk, and the saucer kept clean. I will attend to the file immediately after.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: File can wait, the chai can't. Just drink it, sir, we are all tired of this name confusion.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The file can wait for the morning, but the tea must be drunk now. Thank you.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Drink it before it goes cold, sir. The file will still be there in the morning, but the chai won't be as good.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. The file will wait for the morning, but the chai will not wait for me. I accept the counsel.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: Counsel, sir? You are making a civil servant of me. Just drink the tea, the cold air outside is enough to freeze your thoughts.

records.speaker: Hegel
records.words: You are right, Shri Hegde. I forget that I am a man who must eat, not merely a mind that must think. I accept the tea.

records.speaker: Shri G. Hegde
records.words: There you go. No need to be so dramatic, just grab the saucer. It’s still warm.
